c.v: This stage is about a codebase we did not write: rosbag2, cloned into its own workspace so a source build never sits on top of the debian install, which the project's own guide calls undefined behaviour if the two mix. Building it with its own command builds the whole dependency graph in one pass, and listing the packages afterward gives four layers, storage, the C++ core, the transport nodes and the command line, the same split the bench's own code follows.
The decision worth defending is checking which build a terminal is actually running before trusting anything else.

What this leaves us able to do: run the whole suite the project's own way, then narrow to one test by name from a rebuild of a single package in under a minute; read a unit test next to the fixture that fakes its reader and see exactly what it does and does not exercise; and break a named test on purpose, watch it fail with a message that explains itself, and put the file back with a clean

subs.title: Build rosbag2 and run its tests

c.v: By the end of this session, rosbag2 is built from source in a workspace of its own,
runs from your build rather than from the debian packages, and you have written down how long the build took and what it produced.

The skill here is not rosbag2. It is being able to take a codebase you did not write, build it, run its tests and find your way around it, which is what the first week of a new job looks like and what an interviewer is really asking when they ask about open source. rosbag2 is a good one to practise on for three reasons: the bench already leans on it, so a bug in it is a bug you have met; it is a normal size, about two dozen packages rather than two or two thousand; and it is tested with the same tools the bench uses, so you can read its tests without learning a new framework.
One warning comes from the project itself. Its developer guide says that building rosbag2 from source on top of a debian install of
has undefined behaviour. So this gets a workspace of its own, away from
, and you source one or the other in a terminal and never both.

items.v: Make the workspace and clone the branch that matches your ROS 2:

blocks.text:
mkdir -p ~/rosbag2_ws/src && cd ~/rosbag2_ws/src
git clone https://github.com/ros2/rosbag2.git -b jazzy
cd ~/rosbag2_ws

c.v: The branch matters more than it looks.

is built against the development version of ROS 2 and will fail against Jazzy in ways that have nothing to do with your machine. Every command in the next three topics assumes the branch you cloned here.

items.v: Install what it needs, the way its CI does:

blocks.text:
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
rosdep update
rosdep install --from-paths src --ignore-src -y

items.v: Build it with the project's own command, and time it:

items.v: Prove that the build is the one you are running:

blocks.text:
source ~/rosbag2_ws/install/setup.bash
ros2 pkg prefix rosbag2_transport     # your workspace, not /opt/ros/jazzy
ros2 bag --help

c.v: Open a second terminal, don't source the overlay, and run
. Those two terminals hold two different rosbag2s, and the difference between them is the single commonest cause of an afternoon spent debugging a fix that was never loaded.

items.v: Record and play something with it, so that "it built" becomes "it works":

blocks.text:
ros2 run demo_nodes_cpp talker                       # terminal 1, without the overlay
ros2 bag record -o /tmp/oss_check --topics /chatter   # terminal 2, with the overlay
ros2 bag info /tmp/oss_check                          # terminal 2, after Ctrl+C

c.v: reads a bag your own build recorded. Write the wall time and the package count down now; the summary step needs them.
By the end of this session, rosbag2's tests run on your machine, you have run a single test file on its own, and you can say of one test what it fakes and what it really exercises.

Running someone else's tests is the fastest way to learn what a project believes about itself. The names tell you which behaviours the maintainers thought worth protecting, and the fixtures tell you where they drew the line between a unit test and an integration test. You also need them working before the next topic: a reproduction is only believable if the suite was green before you touched anything.

items.v: Run the suite with the project's own commands:

blocks.text:
cd ~/rosbag2_ws
colcon test --packages-up-to rosbag2 --return-code-on-test-failure
colcon test-result --verbose

c.v: Expect it to take longer than the build and to be noisier. Some of these tests start processes, publish on real topics and wait on timing, which the bench met in its own exchange test. A released branch on a supported platform should come out green. A failure that repeats is a finding; a failure that does not repeat is a flaky test, which is also a finding, and the number of times out of ten is the part a maintainer wants.

items.v: Narrow it down, because the loop above is too slow to work in:

blocks.text:
colcon test --packages-select rosbag2_transport
colcon test-result --verbose --test-result-base build/rosbag2_transport
cd build/rosbag2_transport
ctest -N                                   # the test names, without running them
ctest -R test_play_timing --output-on-failure

runs the whole family. This is the loop for the rest of this track: change one file,

items.v: Learn to find things without reading everything. These four moves answer most questions:

blocks.text:
grep -rn "start-paused" src/rosbag2 --include=*.cpp --include=*.py
git -C src/rosbag2 log --oneline -20 -- rosbag2_transport/src/rosbag2_transport/player.cpp
git -C src/rosbag2 log -S "clock_publish_frequency" --oneline
git -C src/rosbag2 blame -L 100,140 rosbag2_transport/src/rosbag2_transport/player.cpp

c.v: finds where a name is used, and the first log finds who has been changing a file lately.

is the one people forget: it finds the commits where the count of a string changed, so it lands on the commit that introduced an option rather than on every commit that touched the file. From a commit you get its pull request, and from the pull request you get the argument that produced the behaviour you are looking at.
is for one stubborn line, once the other three have failed.

items.v: Prove you can break a test on purpose, which is the only way to know the suite is watching the thing you think it is. Pick a named test from step 2, find the code it exercises, change one number or one condition, rebuild that package alone, and watch that test fail with a message you can read. Then put it back:

blocks.text:
git -C src/rosbag2 status
git -C src/rosbag2 restore rosbag2_transport/src/rosbag2_transport/player.cpp
colcon build --packages-select rosbag2_transport
